question: In May 2022, the Commission published an analysis of existing gaps in Member States’ defence investment policies. This analysis came at the request of European heads of state following the Versailles meeting in March 2022 and was also a concrete initiative under the EU Strategic Compass. It aimed to make future European defence spending as effective as possible. 1.
Can the VP/HR provide an overview of the extent to which Member States have since followed up on this analysis when investing in defence policies?
Has the call for medium- to long-term joint development of new capabilities such as the ‘Eurodrone’ or the modernisation of European anti-access/area denial systems already been acted upon?
answer: The Joint Communication on the Defence Investment Gaps Analysis and Way Forwar d (1) pointed at significant capabilities and industrial gaps, exacerbated by substantial long-term cuts in Member States’ defence spending, as well as fragmented and uncoordinated demand.

Since the start of Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, the defence expenditure of Member States increased by 6% in real terms to EUR 240 billion for 2022 (2). Member States have also increased their use of EU prioritisation and coordination tools such as the Coordinated Annual Review on Defence (CARD) and the Capability Development Plan (CDP) when drawing their national plans (3).

The upcoming CARD aggregated analysis by the European Defence Agency, due for approval in November 2024, will provide an updated overview of the EU defence landscape and allow to observe whether such trends persist. A cooperative ‘Eurodrone’ programme between Germany, Spain, Italy and France is currently in the development phase.

Integrated air and missile defence capabilities, as well as the further development of remotely piloted aircraft systems are part of the capability development priorities recently agreed by Member States. These priorities serve as the central reference for all EU defence initiatives in the short, medium and long-term.
